query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: A rapid thermal annealing (RTA) process applied to an equiatomic FeCoNi‐based high‐entropy thin film deposited on a lattice-mismatched substrate will drive a strain-assisted, directional chemical ordering (for example, toward an L10-type low-symmetry phase) that enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy and thereby significantly increases the coercivity relative to the soft fcc phase normally observed.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited, nearly equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy thin film exhibiting a face-centered cubic (fcc) structure with high saturation magnetization but low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Subject the film to rapid thermal annealing (RTA) while it remains on a substrate that imposes a strong lattice-mismatch (and hence strain) during the annealing process.
generation.conditions: RTA performed under optimized temperature and time conditions (short high-temperature pulses) such that the strain from the lattice-mismatched substrate induces lattice distortion and ordering, while keeping the alloy near equiatomic composition (ensuring configurational entropy ≥1.0R). This is applicable to thin film samples where substrate-induced strain is significant.
generation.structural_mediator: The RTA combined with substrate-induced strain produces a directional lattice distortion and promotes a partial phase transformation from the high-symmetry fcc state to a chemically ordered low-symmetry phase (e.g., L10-like structure), increasing the magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
generation.mechanism: Under RTA the thermal energy drives atomic mobility while the imposed substrate strain biases the ordering in specific crystallographic directions. This produces a lower-symmetry (tetragonally distorted) ordered phase that creates larger energy barriers for domain wall motion, thereby enhancing coercivity without severely compromising the high saturation magnetization inherent to the FeCoNi system.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited fcc FeCoNi baseline (which typically exhibits coercivities on the order of tens of Oe), the RTA-treated film should show a coercivity increased by at least an order of magnitude, owing to the additional magnetic anisotropy induced by the low-symmetry ordered phase.
generation.baseline: FeCoNi-based high-entropy films in the as-deposited fcc state (with low coercivity, e.g., ~10–50 Oe) serve as the baseline.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold in thin film geometries where substrate-induced strain is effective; in bulk samples the same intervention may not achieve the desired ordering due to the absence of such an external strain field. Moreover, the processing window (temperature, time) must be finely tuned to induce ordering without triggering unwanted phase separation.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis combines observations from RTA-induced coercivity increases and ordering in related FeCoNiMnCu systems (e.g., as discussed in PMC11426066 in both the Introduction and Results and Discussion sections) with the concept of strain-driven ordering. The precise magnitude of coercivity enhancement and the detailed nature of the ordered phase in a ternary FeCoNi-based system (as opposed to quaternary/quinary systems) remain to be confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of equiatomic FeCoNi-based thin films on a substrate with a known lattice mismatch. Divide the samples into two groups: one group remains as-deposited (control) and the other undergoes RTA under a range of optimized conditions. Characterize the films by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to probe for the emergence of a low-symmetry (e.g., L10-type) phase. Measure the magnetic hysteresis loops by vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) to quantify changes in coercivity.
measurements: XRD for phase identification and lattice parameter determination
TEM for imaging chemical ordering and lattice distortions
VSM to measure coercivity, saturation magnetization, and anisotropy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If RTA-treated films do not show evidence of a low-symmetry, chemically ordered phase (or exhibit only random strain without directional ordering) and if the coercivity does not increase by at least an order of magnitude compared to the as-deposited baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Certain HEA compositions may exhibit long‐range chemical order through the emergence of multiple sublattices, analogous to high entropy ceramics,[  ] leading to so‐called “high entropy intermetallic” (HEI) compounds.[  ] Previously, transition metal alloys with high anisotropy, such as the L10 phases of FePt and FePd have been achieved by annealing of equiatomic solid solution pre‐cursors.[  ] In the case of metastable high anisotropy phases such as L10 FeNi, unconventional annealing techniques have been employed.[  ] In particular, rapid thermal annealing (RTA) of transition metal alloy films on Si/SiO2 is an effective means of inducing high anisotropy phase formation in solid solution precursors, in part due to the substrate‐induced strain.[  ] In this study, we experimentally demonstrate two thin film HEAs with large coercivity and magnetic anisotropy achieved by RTA. We show that RTA treatment of equiatomic FeCoNiMnCu thin films leads to ≈40‐fold increase in coercivity. By introduction of 50 at.% Pt, we realize an L10 HEI phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy resulting from a reduced lattice symmetry and strong spin‐orbit coupling. The 1–2 orders of magnitude coercivity increase in RTA‐treated samples, compared to the as‐grown ones, suggests the emergence of sizeable magnetic anisotropy in the film. The fact that the continuous 15s RTA sample (Figure 1b) exhibits a 350 Oe coercivity, indicates that the dewetting process and film morphology evolution in some of the samples are not essential to the significant coercivity enhancement. Previous studies on bulk FeCoNiMnCu solid solutions have not found appreciable magnetic anisotropy ascribed to the disordered phase.[ ,  ] Hard magnetic properties in some solid solutions have been attributed to the magnetocrystalline or shape anisotropy of a secondary phase, however, studies of bulk phase‐separated FeCoNiMnCu have not shown large coercivity of the order presented here.[  ] In the present RTA‐treated samples, likely the anisotropic strain has induced lattice and grain distortions or directional chemical order, different from those in bulk systems, and stabilized sizable magnetic anisotropy, similar to that in RTA‐assisted synthesis of L10 FeCuPt.[ ,  ]
